# Contraception

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Obstetrics/gynecology > Fertility, contraception, and reproductive endocrinology > Contraception*

[Original Article Link](/library/rt0fU3)

---

## Summary

Contraception is the prevention of <u>pregnancy</u> through the use of medications, medical devices, or behaviors. Many different contraceptive options (both hormonal and nonhormonal) exist, allowing individuals to choose a method suited to their medical needs and <u>pregnancy</u> prevention priorities; some methods offer additional noncontraceptive benefits. <u>Hormonal contraceptives</u> contain <u>estrogen</u> and/or <u>progestins</u> to prevent <u>ovulation</u>, <u>fertilization</u>, and/or implantation of an embryo. Nonhormonal contraceptives include sterilization, the <u>copper IUD</u>, <u>barrier methods of contraception</u>, and <u>behavioral methods of contraception</u>. The duration of contraception provided ranges from the length of intercourse (e.g., <u>condoms</u>) to years (<u>long-acting reversible contraception</u> such as <u>IUDs</u> and the <u>progestin implant</u>). The choice of contraception involves <u>shared decision-making</u> that balances the individual patient's preferences with the risks of contraceptive use. The US Medical Eligibility Criteria (<u>USMEC</u>) for contraceptive use are used to provide risk-based guidance for individuals with coexisting medical conditions. Although often neglected, easy access to contraception, including <u>emergency contraception</u>, is an important part of medical care for all individuals who require it. Some contraception is available without a prescription; most require a prescription or a <u>health care professional</u> to fit them.

---

## Overview

### Hormonal and <u>nonhormonal contraception</u>




* <u>Hormonal contraception</u>

* Uses <u>progestin</u> with or without <u>estrogen</u> to prevent <u>conception</u> through one or a combination of the following:

* Prevention of <u>ovulation</u>

* Thickening of cervical mucus

* Creation of an inhospitable intrauterine environment

* Examples include the <u>hormonal IUD</u>, <u>combined hormonal contraception</u>, and <u>progestin-only pill</u>, implant, or injection.

* Nonhormonal contraception

* Prevents <u>conception</u> without altering natural <u>hormones</u>

* The mechanism of action depends on the method.

* <u>Copper IUD</u>: creation of an inhospitable intrauterine environment

* Barrier methods: prevention of <u>sperm</u> reaching the <u>uterus</u>

* Behavioral methods: avoidance of sex during the <u>fertile window</u>

* Sterilization: blockage of the passage of <u>gametes</u>





### Overview of methods [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[2]](/library/oB10bj0)[[3]](/library/tuaXGm)




* All methods of contraception are reversible except sterilization.

* Choice of method is tailored to patient preference and comorbid medical conditions.

* For further information, see specific sections.

### Contraceptive <u>efficacy</u>




The <u>efficacy</u> of contraceptive methods is reported as the contraceptive failure rate, i.e., the percentage of individuals who become pregnant within 12 months of initiating a contraceptive method. [[11]](/library/QlWu9l0)




* Failure rate with typical use: includes all individuals using that method regardless of whether it is used correctly and/or consistently [[11]](/library/QlWu9l0)

* <u>Failure rate with perfect use</u>, also called the <u>Pearl index</u>: includes only individuals who use the method correctly and consistently; mainly used in clinical studies  [[11]](/library/QlWu9l0)





> [!TIP]
> 85% of female individuals currently using a contraceptive method would become pregnant within 1 year if contraception were stopped. [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)

## Approach to initiating contraceptives

### Selecting a method [[12]](/library/jD1_VQ0)[[13]](/library/YyWndL0)




* Assess the individual's:

* Future reproductive goals

* Previous experience with contraception

* <u>Past medical history</u> to determine <u>USMEC for contraceptive use</u> (may require a limited <u>physical exam</u>) 

* Some contraceptive methods are contraindicated for patients with select medical conditions.

* Encourage patients with <u>conditions that increase the risk of complications in pregnancy</u> to use <u>LARCs</u>.

* Individual contraceptive preferences

* Outline which methods an individual can safely use.

* Explain a combination of methods may be necessary to meet all of an individual's needs, e.g.:

* <u>Condoms</u> for <u>STI</u> protection

* AND <u>LARC</u> for <u>highly effective contraception</u>





> [!TIP]
> Patient preference, comorbid medical conditions, and availability will affect the choice of contraception.




### Prescribing contraception [[12]](/library/jD1_VQ0)




* Avoid barriers to contraceptive use.

* Use a <u>quick start approach</u> rather than waiting until the next <u>menstrual cycle</u>.

* Use <u>patient history</u> to <u>reasonably exclude pregnancy</u> rather than requiring a <u>pregnancy test</u>.

* Offer <u>STI testing</u>, but do not require individuals to wait for results to initiate contraception.  [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Do not require a routine <u>pelvic examination</u> and <u>Pap smear</u>.

* Offer <u>telehealth</u> appointments for <u>initiation of contraception</u> and repeat prescriptions, when possible. [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)

* Prescribe a one-year supply of contraceptives. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Provide basic patient education (e.g., <u>management of unscheduled bleeding</u>, <u>missed or delayed contraception</u>).

* Advise patients to return at any point to discuss concerns or change contraceptive method.





> [!TIP]
> All methods of contraception can be initiated at any time during <u>the menstrual cycle</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

## U.S. Medical Eligibility Criteria (USMEC) for contraceptive use

The following information is used by <u>health care providers</u> for individuals with specific medical conditions or medically relevant factors (e.g., age) to estimate individualized levels of risk versus benefit when choosing a method of contraception.




### Category definitions [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[15]](/library/pidLsp0)




* USMEC category 1: no limitations on use

* USMEC category 2: benefits generally outweigh risks

* USMEC category 3: risks often outweigh benefits (<u>relative contraindication</u>)

* USMEC category 4: risks outweigh benefits (<u>absolute contraindication</u>)





> [!TIP]
> Category definitions only apply to contraception indications and do not apply when contraceptives are used to treat other medical conditions (e.g., <u>ovarian cysts</u>). [[15]](/library/pidLsp0)




### Contraindications for contraceptive methods [[15]](/library/pidLsp0)




* Recommend alternative forms of contraception to individuals with <u>absolute contraindications</u>.

* For patients with <u>relative contraindications</u>, these methods may be used following <u>shared decision-making</u> if the patient:

* Cannot use alternative forms of contraception

* Does not wish to use alternative forms of contraception

* Consult <u>USMEC</u> guidelines for more detailed information.

## Surgical sterilization

### General principles [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[20]](/library/byWHdL0)




* Sterilization is only indicated in patients who desire or, for medical reasons, require a permanent end to <u>fertility</u>.

* Individual <u>autonomy</u> is of utmost importance.

* Highly effective at preventing <u>pregnancy</u> [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Does not protect against <u>STIs</u> (but may decrease risk of <u>PID</u> in females)   [[21]](/library/YmWnVN0)





> [!TIP]
> If indicated for medical reasons, other procedures also result in sterilization, e.g., <u>hysterectomy</u> and/or bilateral <u>oophorectomy</u> in females and bilateral <u>orchiectomy</u> in males.




### Bilateral tubal ligation [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Description

* A surgical procedure in which both <u>fallopian tubes</u> are permanently blocked or severed

* Prevents <u>fertilization</u> by removing the connection between the <u>uterus</u> and <u>ovaries</u>

* Generally performed under <u>local anesthesia</u> with or without sedation

* Failure rates: 0.5% (perfect and typical use) [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)

* Available methods  [[21]](/library/YmWnVN0)

* <u>Laparoscopy</u> or minilaparotomy

* <u>Tubal ligation</u> with or without <u>salpingectomy</u>

* Electrocoagulation of the oviduct

* <u>Clipping</u> or <u>banding</u> of the <u>fallopian tubes</u>

* Postprocedure counseling: No <u>backup contraception</u> is required.

* Complications [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Hemorrhage

* Infection

* If <u>pregnancy</u> occurs, there is an elevated risk of it being <u>ectopic</u>, but the <u>absolute risk</u> of an <u>ectopic pregnancy</u> is extremely low.  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)





> [!TIP]
> Notify patients that age and waiting period restrictions may apply depending on local protocols. [[22]](/library/cJWaGm0)




### Vasectomy [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




* Description

* A minimally invasive procedure, performed under <u>local anesthesia</u> resulting in permanent occlusion of the <u>vas deferens</u>; can be performed by: [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Division of the <u>vas deferens</u>  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Intraluminal cautery to induce <u>fibrosis</u>

* <u>Sperm</u> cannot enter the ejaculate, which prevents <u>fertilization</u>.

* Failure rates: perfect use 0.10%, typical use 0.15%  [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Postprocedure counseling: <u>Backup contraception</u> is required until <u>azoospermia</u> is confirmed with a <u>sperm</u> sample 8–16 weeks after <u>surgery</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Complications [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* <u>Hematoma</u>

* <u>Surgical site infection</u>

* Sperm granuloma: a collection of <u>sperm</u> due to leakage from the <u>vas deferens</u> into the surrounding <u>interstitium</u>; occurs in ∼ 40% of men following <u>vasectomy</u> [[23]](/library/ZrWZf50)

* Postvasectomy pain syndrome: the accumulation of testicular fluid in the <u>epididymis</u> after a <u>vasectomy</u> resulting in a chronic, dull, aching <u>pain</u> in the <u>testes</u>

## Intrauterine devices

This information pertains to using <u>IUDs</u> as routine contraception. Additional information on <u>IUD</u> use is available in “<u>Emergency contraception</u>.”




### General principles




* <u>IUDs</u> are small T-shaped devices that are inserted into the <u>uterus</u>.

* Can be nonhormonal (<u>copper IUD</u>) or contain <u>progestin</u> (<u>hormonal IUD</u>)

* Used for both regular and <u>emergency contraception</u>  [[24]](/library/Fa1gm20)

* Mainly thought to work by preventing <u>fertilization</u>, but may also decrease the likelihood of implantation

* Reversible and highly effective as are user-independent

* Can be used by <u>nulliparous</u> or parous individuals  [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Last between 3–12 years

* May provide additional noncontraceptive benefits of IUDs, e.g.: [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[25]](/library/XpW9Lm0)

* Reduced risk of cervical and <u>endometrial cancers</u> [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Decreased <u>menstrual pain</u> and bleeding (<u>progestin IUDs</u>); see also “<u>Noncontraceptive benefits of progestins</u>.” [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[25]](/library/XpW9Lm0)





![Intrauterine device in situ](media/u5scadhbvskjyhjj46quoigh.jpg)

Intrauterine device in situ




### Types of <u>IUDs</u>




#### Copper intrauterine device [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Description

* <u>Hormone</u>-free, <u>copper</u>-containing <u>intrauterine device</u>

* Longest-lasting reversible method of contraception:

* <u>FDA</u>-approved up to 10 years after insertion

* Studies show <u>effectiveness</u> for up to 12 years [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Mechanism of action [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)[[25]](/library/XpW9Lm0)

* Cu+ ions create localized inflammation that decreases <u>sperm</u> viability and function (prevents <u>fertilization</u>). [[26]](/library/yIWd250)

* May decrease the likelihood of implantation

* Failure rates: ∼ 0.6% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)





> [!WARNING]
> The <u>copper IUD</u> may cause heavy and prolonged menstrual bleeding, especially during the first 3–6 months after placement. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




#### Hormonal IUD [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Description

* Long-term, reversible <u>levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine device</u> (contains no <u>estrogen</u>)

* <u>FDA</u> approved for 3–8 years after insertion (depending on the <u>IUD</u>)  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Mechanism of action: local effects of <u>progestin</u> [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)[[25]](/library/XpW9Lm0)

* Prevents <u>fertilization</u> via:

* Cervical mucous changes  block the <u>sperm</u> from reaching an <u>oocyte</u>

* Decreased <u>sperm</u> function and viability

* Decreases the likelihood of implantation via changes to the <u>endometrial</u> lining [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)

* Unlike systemic <u>progestins</u>, <u>progestin IUDs</u> do not reliably suppress <u>ovulation</u>.

* Failure rates: 0.1–0.4%  [[2]](/library/oB10bj0)[[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)





> [!TIP]
> 40–50% of individuals with <u>progestin-containing IUD</u> will become amenorrheic after 2 years. [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




### Initiation of IUDs [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)[[27]](/library/_a15M20)




#### Preplacement evaluation




* Ensure the patient does not have contraindications to <u>copper IUDs</u>/contraindications to <u>hormonal IUDs</u>.

* Perform a <u>bimanual exam</u> and speculum-assisted visualization of the <u>cervix</u>.

* Obtain <u>pregnancy test</u>;  only if unable to <u>reasonably exclude pregnancy</u>.  [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Offer routine <u>STI screening</u>; <u>STI testing</u> is not required prior to placement.





#### Procedure




* Performed at an outpatient visit

* Can be performed during any part of <u>the menstrual cycle</u> [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Offer <u>analgesia</u> to all patients. [[28]](/library/3wdSiH0)[[29]](/library/GLdB_q0)

* Procedural <u>pain</u>

* Topical <u>lidocaine</u> spray DOSAGE [[28]](/library/3wdSiH0)

* OR <u>lidocaine</u>-<u>prilocaine</u> cream DOSAGE [[28]](/library/3wdSiH0)

* OR <u>paracervical block</u>

* Postprocedural <u>pain</u>: <u>NSAIDs</u> (for dosages, see “<u>Oral analgesia</u>”) [[28]](/library/3wdSiH0)

* If <u>IUD</u> insertion is unsuccessful, consider <u>misoprostol</u>.  [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>NSAIDs</u> may decrease postprocedural <u>pain</u> but do not provide sufficient <u>analgesia</u> for <u>IUD</u> insertion when used alone. [[28]](/library/3wdSiH0)




#### Postprocedure counseling




* Educate patients on the <u>adverse effects and complications of IUDs</u>. [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Advise continued <u>condom</u> use for <u>STI</u> protection. [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* Discuss the consideration of <u>backup contraception</u> for the first 7 days.  [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)[[30]](/library/D9W1pn0)

* Checking for <u>IUD</u> strings to confirm correct placement.

* Advise patients that return to <u>fertility</u> may be immediate if the device is removed or expelled.





#### Follow up




At subsequent routine visits:  [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




* Ensure strings are present (first routine visit)  [[31]](/library/ABWRWL0)

* Ask about side effects and patient concerns.





### Adverse effects and complications of IUDs [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Adverse effects: <u>pain</u> and menstrual changes (typically resolve within 3–6 months) ;  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* All <u>IUDs</u>: temporary cramping and discomfort

* <u>Hormonal IUD</u>: <u>abnormal uterine bleeding</u> (e.g., spotting, irregular <u>menses</u>), <u>amenorrhea</u>

* <u>Copper IUD</u>: <u>heavy menstrual bleeding</u>, <u>dysmenorrhea</u>

* Complications [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)[[32]](/library/xIWEU50)

* Expulsion  [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)

* Uterine perforation  [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)

* If <u>pregnancy</u> occurs, there is an elevated risk of it being <u>ectopic</u>, but the <u>absolute risk</u> of an <u>ectopic pregnancy</u> is extremely low.  [[5]](/library/dlWoDl0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

## Hormonal contraception

### General principles




* <u>Hormonal contraception</u> offers some of the most reliable protection against <u>pregnancy</u>.

* <u>Noncontraceptive benefits of hormonal contraception</u> can also be used to treat a variety of medical conditions.

* Multiple options of varying durations exist:

* Long-acting contraception: <u>progestin IUD</u>, <u>progestin implant</u>

* Intermediate-acting contraception: <u>depot medroxyprogesterone acetate</u>

* Short-acting contraception: <u>CHCs</u> or <u>POPs</u>

* For individuals with <u>contraindications to CHCs</u>, <u>progestin-only contraception</u> can often be used.

* Patients with <u>contraindications to progestins</u> should be offered <u>nonhormonal contraception</u>.





### Mechanism of action for hormonal contraceptives




* <u>Estrogen</u>: suppresses release of <u>GnRH</u> from the <u>hypothalamus</u> → ↓ release of <u>pituitary</u> <u>gonadotropins</u> (<u>FSH</u>, <u>LH</u>) [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Decreased <u>FSH</u> → prevents ovarian <u>folliculogenesis</u> [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Decreased <u>LH</u> → inhibition of <u>ovulation</u> [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Progestin: synthetic <u>progesterone</u> → [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Inhibits <u>GnRH</u> and <u>LH</u> secretion → suppressed <u>ovulation</u> (main contraceptive mechanism) [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Inhibits <u>endometrial</u> <u>proliferation</u> → decreases chance of embryo implantation [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Changes cervical mucus (↓ volume and ↑ viscosity) and impairs <u>fallopian tube</u> <u>peristalsis</u> → inhibits <u>sperm</u> migration and embryo implantation [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Inhibits follicular maturation





### Noncontraceptive benefits of hormonal contraception [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[33]](/library/BIWzU50)




* Noncontraceptive benefits of CHCs

* Regulation of <u>menstrual cycles</u>

* Decreased menstrual bleeding, including induced <u>amenorrhea</u>  [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Less painful <u>menstruation</u>

* Decrease in <u>hormone</u> level fluctuations

* Decreased risk of <u>endometrial</u> and <u>ovarian cancers</u>  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* <u>Ovarian cyst</u> prevention

* Reduction of free <u>testosterone</u>

* May increase <u>bone mineral density</u>

* Noncontraceptive benefits of progestins: The main benefits are a result of <u>endometrial</u> <u>atrophy</u>.

* Decreased <u>menstrual pain</u>

* Reduced menstrual bleeding, inducing induced <u>amenorrhea</u> (varies by formulation)

* Decreased risk of <u>endometrial cancer</u>





> [!TIP]
> If patients desire <u>amenorrhea</u>, consider using <u>CHCs</u> (continuous use), <u>DMPA</u>, a high-dose <u>norethindrone</u> acetate <u>POP</u>, or a <u>progestin IUD</u>. [[33]](/library/BIWzU50)[[34]](/library/AIWR250)

---

## Combined hormonal contraception

### General principles




* <u>CHCs</u> provide highly effective, short-acting, reversible contraception if taken perfectly.

* Contains a combination of <u>estrogen</u> and <u>progestins</u>

* <u>Ovulation</u> is suppressed via systemic <u>estrogen</u> with all forms of <u>CHCs</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* More <u>contraindications to CHCs</u> exist than to other forms of contraception.

* <u>CHCs</u> are taken daily, weekly, or monthly, and <u>efficacy</u> is often affected by adherence.





### Noncontraceptive benefits for <u>CHCs</u>




<u>Noncontraceptive benefits of CHCs</u> mean they can be used to treat multiple gynecological and nongynecological conditions, e.g.:  [[33]](/library/BIWzU50)[[35]](/library/arWQf50)




* <u>Polycystic ovary syndrome</u> (<u>PCOS</u>)

* <u>Endometriosis</u>

* <u>Abnormal uterine bleeding</u>, <u>heavy menstrual bleeding</u> [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* <u>Primary dysmenorrhea</u>

* <u>Mittelschmerz</u>

* Benign <u>ovarian cysts</u> [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* <u>Heavy menstrual bleeding</u> associated with <u>uterine leiomyomas</u> [[36]](/library/XAc9RU0)

* <u>Hyperandrogenism</u>, including <u>hirsutism</u> and <u>acne</u> (see “<u>Hormonal therapy for acne</u>”)  [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)

* Other conditions temporally associated with <u>menstruation</u>

* Menstrual-related <u>migraine</u> (without <u>aura</u>)  [[37]](/library/NqW-Am0)

* <u>Premenstrual dysphoric disorder</u> (<u>PMDD</u>)

* Menstrual <u>acne</u>





### Types of <u>CHCs</u> [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




| Overview of combined hormonal contraceptives |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | Additional information |
| <br>Combined oral contraceptives (<u>COCs</u>) [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br> | <br><br>* An oral pill that contains <u>estrogen</u> and <u>progestin</u> and is taken daily  [[38]](/library/0Qdeup0)<br><br>* Common options  [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[39]](/library/Oy1I2j0)<br><br>* <u>Norethindrone</u> acetate/<u>ethinyl estradiol</u><br><br>* <u>Drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol</u><br><br>* <u>Norethindrone</u>/<u>ethinyl estradiol</u><br><br>* <u>Drospirenone</u>/estetrol<br><br>* <u>Levonorgestrel</u>/<u>ethinyl estradiol</u><br><br>* Desogestrel/<u>ethinyl estradiol</u><br><br>* No consensus on preferred <u>COCs</u>; some specialists recommend the following approach:<br><br>* No patient preference: Initiate a low-dose (i.e., 30 mcg of <u>ethinylestradiol</u>) monophasic pill with <u>levonorgestrel</u>  [[40]](/library/70d4ho0)[[41]](/library/H0dKho0)<br><br>* Consider switching to alternative options based on adverse effects.<br><br>* Failure rate: perfect use 0.3%, typical use 9% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* If desired, <u>COC</u> use may be extended or used continuously. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br><br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> <u>CHCs</u> can be used continuously, avoiding a scheduled withdrawal bleed, but extended or continuous use is associated with an increased <u>incidence</u> of <u>breakthrough bleeding</u>. [[43]](/library/iCWJ7n0)




### Initiation of <u>CHCs</u>




* Provide adequate counseling to ensure this is the most appropriate option for the patient (see “<u>Approach to initiating contraceptives</u>”).

* Ensure the patient has no <u>contraindications to CHCs</u>.

* Determine if the patient requires <u>backup contraception</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* ≤ 5 days from day 0 of <u>LMP</u>: <u>Backup contraception</u> is not required.

* > 5 days from day 0 of <u>LMP</u> or > 7 days after <u>miscarriage</u> or abortion: Recommend <u>backup contraception</u> for 7 days.

* Inform patients about the common <u>adverse effects of CHCs</u>.

* Ensure patients know what to do if <u>contraception is late or missed</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Educate all patients on <u>contraindications to CHCs</u> and advise patients to stop <u>CHCs</u> immediately and consult a healthcare professional if any contraindications develop.




### Adverse effects of CHCs [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




Mainly related to the <u>adverse effects of estrogen</u>, e.g.:




* Common

* <u>Headaches</u>

* <u>Breast</u> tenderness

* GI symptoms: <u>nausea</u>, <u>GERD</u>  [[44]](/library/8UcOUb0)

* Mood swings

* Irregular bleeding  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Worsening <u>acne</u>  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Serious (rare)

* <u>Venous thromboembolism</u> (<u>VTE</u>)  [[45]](/library/HDaKf5)

* Cardiovascular conditions: <u>hypertension</u>, <u>stroke</u>, <u>myocardial infarction</u>

* <u>Hepatocellular adenoma</u> development  [[46]](/library/KCWUGn0)





> [!TIP]
> Many patients believe weight gain is a side effect of <u>CHCs</u>, however, studies have not shown an association. [[47]](/library/hyWcUL0)

---

## Progestin-only contraception

### General overview [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[33]](/library/BIWzU50)




* <u>Progestin</u>-only contraceptives are highly effective.

* May be an option for individuals with <u>contraindications to CHCs</u>

* Reversible duration ranges from short-acting (daily tablets) to long-acting (implants and <u>hormonal IUDs</u>)

* Can be used to manage: 

* <u>Abnormal uterine bleeding</u>

* <u>Primary dysmenorrhea</u>

* <u>Endometriosis</u>





### Types of <u>progestin-only contraception</u> [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




| <br>Overview of progestin-only contraception [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | Additional information |
| <br>Progestin-only contraceptive pills (<u>POPs</u>) [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)<br> | <br><br>* Short-acting, reversible, low-dose <u>progestin</u> pill<br><br>* Options<br><br>* Taken continuously   [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br><br>* <u>Norethindrone</u> DOSAGE<br><br>* Norgestrel DOSAGE<br><br>* Monthly pause  : <u>drospirenone</u> DOSAGE [[48]](/library/hCWc7n0)<br><br>* Failure rate: perfect use 0.3%, typical use 9% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Drospirenone</u> can be taken up to 24 hours late without reduced <u>efficacy</u>.<br><br>* In the US, norgestrel is available over the counter. [[49]](/library/OqWIAm0)<br><br><br> |

[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br><br>* Black box warning for potential decreased <u>bone mineral density</u>  [[9]](/library/6B1jbj0)[[15]](/library/pidLsp0)<br><br>* Encourage the <u>recommended daily intake of vitamin D</u> and <u>calcium</u>. [[9]](/library/6B1jbj0)[[51]](/library/TrW6g50)<br><br><br> |
| <br><u>Progestin IUD</u> [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br> | <br>* See “<u>Hormonal IUD</u>.”<br><br> |  |

### Initiating <u>progestin-only contraception</u>




For patients wishing to use the <u>hormonal IUD</u>, see “<u>Initiating an IUD</u>.”




* Provide adequate counseling to ensure this is the most appropriate option for the patient (see “<u>Approach to initiating contraceptives</u>”).

* Ensure the patient has no <u>contraindications to progestins</u>.

* Determine if the patient requires <u>backup contraception</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* ≤ 5 days from day 0 of <u>LMP</u>: <u>Backup contraception</u> is not required.

* > 5 days from day 0 of <u>LMP</u>: Recommend <u>backup contraception</u> for patients starting <u>POPs</u>.

* > 7 days from day 0 of <u>LMP</u>: Recommend <u>backup contraception</u> for 7 days for patients starting <u>DMPA</u> or implant.

* > 7 days after <u>miscarriage</u> or abortion: Recommend <u>backup contraception</u> for all methods.

* Inform patients about common <u>adverse effects of progestins</u>.

* Ensure patients know what to do if <u>contraception is late or missed</u>.





### Adverse effects of progestins [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Irregular <u>menstrual cycles</u>, <u>amenorrhea</u>, <u>breakthrough bleeding</u>

* GI symptoms: abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>nausea</u>

* <u>Dizziness</u>

* <u>Headaches</u>

* Mood changes

* <u>Breast</u> tenderness

* <u>Follicular cysts</u> (in nonbreastfeeding female individuals)

* Delayed return to <u>fertility</u> (with <u>DMPA</u> use)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Progestin-only contraceptive</u> methods are commonly believed to cause weight gain; however, studies have not shown an association. [[52]](/library/Nbd-Fo0)

## Barrier methods of contraception

### General principles [[53]](/library/Ly1wfj0)




* Barrier methods of contraception prevent <u>fertilization</u> by blocking the <u>sperm</u> from reaching an <u>oocyte</u>.

* <u>Condoms</u> provide additional protection against <u>STIs</u>.

* Some forms are available without prescription

* May be used as a primary or adjunctive method of contraception

* <u>Efficacy</u> can be low.

* Even with perfect use, barrier methods are less effective than <u>hormonal contraception</u> or <u>IUDs</u>.

* Improper application and <u>poor adherence</u> are common and can reduce <u>efficacy</u> further.





> [!TIP]
> Because <u>barrier methods of contraception</u> must be utilized with each sexual encounter, there is a high risk of <u>poor adherence</u>.




### Types of <u>barrier methods of contraception</u> [[3]](/library/tuaXGm)[[4]](/library/4B13aj0)




#### Condoms [[3]](/library/tuaXGm)[[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Two types exist:

* External condom: a thin sheath of material (e.g., latex, polyisoprene) that covers the <u>penis</u> [[53]](/library/Ly1wfj0)

* Internal condom: a thin sheath of material inserted into the <u>vagina</u> (or <u>rectum</u>)

* Prevent most <u>sexually transmitted infections</u>, including <u>HIV</u> (excluding lambskin <u>condoms</u>)

* To avoid breakage or misplacement: [[53]](/library/Ly1wfj0)

* Use with lubricants (water or silicone-based); oil-based lubricants should never be used with latex <u>condoms</u>

* Avoid simultaneous use of internal and <u>external condoms</u>

* Failure rates

* <u>External condom</u>: perfect use 2%, typical use 18% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)

* <u>Internal condom</u>: perfect 5%, typical 25% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)





> [!TIP]
> Ineffective placement is more likely with <u>internal condoms</u> compared to the <u>external condom</u> as insertion may be uncomfortable and difficult for some individuals. [[53]](/library/Ly1wfj0)




![Female condom (internal condom)](media/g4g0lsn6gf9cphlzrmkkerug.jpg)

Female condom (internal condom)




#### <u>Contraceptive diaphragms</u>, sponges, and <u>cervical caps</u> [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Devices placed inside the <u>vagina</u> to prevent semen from reaching the <u>cervix</u>

* Used with <u>spermicide</u> (or <u>contraceptive gel</u> for patients using the contraceptive diaphragm)

* Must remain in place for at least 6 hours after intercourse; can be inserted 6 hours or more prior to intercourse.  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[10]](/library/PB1Waj0)

* Contraindicated in patients with the following characteristics: [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* History of <u>toxic shock syndrome</u>

* <u>HIV</u> or at <u>high risk for HIV infection</u>

* <u>Contraceptive diaphragm</u> and caps:< 6 weeks postpartum or post-<u>second trimester</u> abortion

* Adverse effects

* <u>Urinary retention</u> leading to <u>UTI</u>  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* <u>Toxic shock syndrome</u>  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)





| Overview of <u>contraceptive diaphragms</u>, sponges, and caps |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Description | Failure rate |
| <br>Contraceptive diaphragm [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[10]](/library/PB1Waj0)<br> | <br><br>* Large dome-shaped device made of latex or plastic<br><br>* Used with <u>spermicide</u> or <u>contraceptive gel</u><br><br>* Options:<br><br>* Professionally fitted <u>contraceptive diaphragm</u> (multiple sizes available)<br><br>* Single-size non-fitted <u>contraceptive diaphragm</u> (requires prescription)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Perfect use 6% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)<br><br>* Typical use 12% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)<br><br><br> |

> Do not use oil-based lubricants with latex <u>contraceptive diaphragms</u> or caps. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

#### Topical barrier methods [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[54]](/library/sCWttn0)




* <u>Spermicide</u> and contraceptive gels are placed in the <u>vagina</u> to prevent <u>sperm</u> from reaching the <u>uterus</u>.

* Inserted prior to sexual intercourse, either with other forms of <u>barrier contraception</u> (e.g., <u>contraceptive diaphragm</u>) or alone.

* Advise patients not to douche afterward as this decreases <u>efficacy</u> and increases the risk of <u>STIs</u>.

* Adverse effects include vaginal irritation.





##### Spermicide [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* A chemical (usually nonoxynol-9) inserted in the <u>vagina</u> prior to sexual intercourse to damage <u>sperm</u> cells  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Available over the counter as gels, creams, foams, films, and suppositories

* Insertion time prior to intercourse and duration of action vary by formulation.  [[55]](/library/SxWyDn0)

* Failure rate: perfect use 18%, typical use ∼ 28% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)

* Use is contraindicated in individuals with <u>HIV</u> or <u>at risk for HIV infection</u>.





##### Contraceptive gel [[54]](/library/sCWttn0)




* A prescription-only gel inserted into the <u>vagina</u> to create an inhospitable environment for <u>sperm</u>

* Insert up to 1 hour prior to sexual intercourse

* Failure rate: perfect use ∼ 4%, typical use 11–14% [[54]](/library/sCWttn0)

* May be used with <u>condoms</u> and <u>contraceptive diaphragms</u>

* Avoid in individuals with:

* <u>Recurrent urinary tract infections</u>

* <u>Urinary tract</u> abnormalities

* A <u>vaginal ring</u> for contraception

---

## Behavioral methods of contraception

### General principles [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




* Behavioral methods of contraception are usually less effective than most other methods of contraception.

* Individuals may choose to use behavioral methods of contraception because of:

* A preference for a natural method of contraception

* The desire or need to avoid <u>hormonal contraception</u>

* Cost as behavioral methods are a free form of contraception.





### Types of behavioral methods of contraception [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




| <br>Overview of behavioral methods of contraception [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br> |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  |  | <br><br>Description<br> | Additional information |
| <br><u>Fertility awareness-based methods</u> [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br> |  | <br><br>* A method of contraception that estimates when a female individual is likely to be ovulating so that intercourse can be avoided (or <u>barrier contraception</u> used) during this <u>fertile window</u>.<br><br>* Failure rate: perfect use < 1–5%, typical use 2–23% [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* High risk of error<br><br>* Requires partner cooperation<br><br>* Requires regular periods<br><br><br> |
| <br>Lactational amenorrhea [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[56]](/library/0xXeEZ0)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Breastfeeding</u> induces <u>amenorrhea</u> and suppresses <u>ovulation</u>.<br><br>* Mechanism thought to be related to: <u>nipple</u> stimulation → ↑ <u>prolactin</u> and disruption of pulsatile <u>GnRH</u> secretion → ↓ <u>LH</u> surge→ suppression of <u>ovulation</u> [[57]](/library/-IWD250)<br><br>* Failure rate: perfect use 1%, typical use < 2% [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)<br><br><br> | <br>* All of the following criteria must be met. | <br>Coitus interruptus [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)[[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[58]](/library/jy1_Uj0)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Penis</u> is withdrawn from the <u>vagina</u> before <u>ejaculation</u>.<br><br>* Failure rate: perfect use 4%, typical use 22% [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)<br><br><br> | <br><br>* Can be used at any time in the cycle<br><br>* High risk of error<br><br>* Requires partner cooperation<br><br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Vaginal douching</u> is not recommended as a form of contraception because of limited <u>efficacy</u> and adverse effects including increased risk of <u>STIs</u>, <u>PID</u>, vaginal infections, and <u>ectopic pregnancy</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[59]](/library/Py1W2j0)




![Menstrual cycle](media/z6wl5lyvfs6krtbftz7umiye.jpg)

Menstrual cycle

## Fertility awareness-based methods

### General principles




* <u>Fertility</u> awareness-based methods estimate when a female individual is likely to be ovulating and fertile.

* When used for contraception, individuals avoid unprotected sex during the <u>fertile window</u> to decrease the chance of <u>conception</u>.

* May be based on calendar dates or symptoms suggestive of <u>ovulation</u>

* User dependent; typical use failure rate can be high.





> [!TIP]
> Some patients use mobile apps to track <u>fertility</u>; <u>efficacy</u> for contraception is unclear. [[60]](/library/9CWN8n0)




### Calendar methods [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[61]](/library/SIWyX50)




* Description: Count the days since the <u>last menstrual period</u> to estimate when <u>ovulation</u> is likely. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Basis for method: <u>Ovulation</u> occurs ∼14 days before the next <u>menstrual period</u>. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* <u>Fertile window</u>: Several methods exist for calculating the <u>fertile window</u>.

* Standard days method: If <u>menstrual cycles</u> are consistently between 26 and 32 days, avoid unprotected intercourse between days 8 and 19. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Calendar <u>rhythm method</u>: depends on the length of the individual's <u>menstrual cycles</u>  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Start of <u>fertile window</u>: length of shortest <u>menstrual cycle</u> minus 18 days

* End of <u>fertile window</u>: length of longest <u>menstrual cycle</u> minus 11 days

* Failure rate: perfect use 5%, typical use 12% [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Caveat: Use carefully or delay starting <u>calendar methods</u> in individuals without regular <u>menstrual cycles</u>.  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)





### Symptom-based methods [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[61]](/library/SIWyX50)




* Description: : Symptoms (e.g., cervical mucus, body temperature, <u>breast</u> tenderness) related to <u>menstrual cycle</u> <u>hormone</u> fluctuations are used to estimate when <u>ovulation</u> is likely.

* Caveat: Use carefully or delay starting symptom-based methods in individuals with: [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Recent <u>pregnancy</u> (due to hormonal changes)

* Irregular <u>menstrual cycles</u>

* An acute or chronic condition that alters body temperature

* Medications that alter cervical secretions or body temperature





#### Cervical mucus methods [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[61]](/library/SIWyX50)




* Description: Check for cervical mucus at least once a day and monitor changes to estimate when <u>ovulation</u> is likely.

* Basis for method [[61]](/library/SIWyX50)

* Prior to <u>ovulation</u>, cervical mucus increases and becomes thin, stretchy, and slippery.

* Following <u>ovulation</u>, cervical mucus decreases and becomes thicker and sticky.

* <u>Fertile window</u>

* <u>TwoDay method</u>: from the onset of cervical mucus until 2 consecutive “dry” days [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* <u>Ovulation</u> method: from the onset of cervical mucus until 4 days after the peak of cervical mucus secretions  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Failure rate: perfect use 3–4%, typical use 14–23% [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)





> [!WARNING]
> While unprotected intercourse is considered safe between the end of <u>menstruation</u> and before cervical mucus appears, avoid 2 consecutive days of intercourse so that residual semen can disappear and not be confused with cervical mucus. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




#### Basal body temperature method [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[61]](/library/SIWyX50)




* Description: Measure the body temperature daily upon first awakening to estimate when <u>ovulation</u> is likely.

* Basis for method: After <u>ovulation</u>, the <u>corpus luteum</u> produces <u>progesterone</u>, which increases body temperature by 0.4–1 °F. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[62]](/library/kIYm1q)

* <u>Fertile window</u>: day 1 until 3 days following the temperature increase [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[61]](/library/SIWyX50)

* Failure rate: no reliable information

* Caveat: affected by conditions that alter body temperature (e.g., <u>fever</u>)





#### Symptothermal method [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[59]](/library/Py1W2j0)[[61]](/library/SIWyX50)




* Description: A combination of the <u>basal body temperature method</u>, <u>cervical mucus method</u>, and other symptoms of <u>ovulation</u> (e.g., <u>breast</u> <u>sensitivity</u>, <u>mittelschmerz</u>) [[4]](/library/4B13aj0)

* <u>Fertile window</u>: from day 1 of <u>menstruation</u> until both of the following have occurred

* 3 days have passed since the <u>basal body temperature</u> increase

* 4 days after peak cervical mucus  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

* Failure rate: perfect use < 1%, typical use 2% [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)

---

## Troubleshooting

Discussion of common issues with contraception should be part of contraceptive counseling for all patients. Consider provision of <u>emergency contraception</u> in advance to patients using less reliable methods of contraception. [[63]](/library/_CW5un0)

---

## Emergency contraception

### General principles [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[63]](/library/_CW5un0)[[68]](/library/2Y1To20)




* <u>Emergency contraception</u> is used to prevent <u>pregnancy</u> following unprotected or inadequately protected intercourse.

* Effective for up to 5 days after intercourse

* Works by disrupting <u>ovulation</u> or <u>fertilization</u>

* Not a form of abortion as does not disrupt established <u>pregnancies</u>

* Options include the <u>IUD</u> and <u>emergency contraceptive pills</u>.

* Choice is based on patient weight and preference for ongoing contraception.





### Initiation of <u>emergency contraception</u> [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)[[68]](/library/2Y1To20)[[69]](/library/WY1PL20)




* Obtain a <u>pregnancy test</u> if unable to <u>reasonably exclude pregnancy</u>.

* Discuss available methods with the individual and evaluate for contraindications.

* Preferred (due to <u>efficacy</u>): <u>IUD</u> or <u>ulipristal acetate</u>

* Alternative: <u>levonorgestrel</u> pill (preferably within 72 hours) or <u>Yuzpe regimen</u>  [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* Preferentially consider placing an <u>IUD</u> for individuals who:

* Desire an <u>IUD</u> for long-term contraception

* Have a <u>BMI</u> ≥ 25 or have a body weight of > 85 kg â¥ 70 kg (â¥ 154 lb) [[27]](/library/_a15M20)[[63]](/library/_CW5un0)[[69]](/library/WY1PL20)

* If using <u>emergency contraceptive pills</u>, especially the <u>Yuzpe regimen</u>, consider prophylactic <u>antiemetics</u>.  [[70]](/library/cpWaom0)

* Provide <u>ongoing management after emergency contraception</u>.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Emergency contraception</u> should be initiated as soon as possible to maximize <u>efficacy</u>. [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)




### Types of emergency contraception




#### IUD for emergency contraception [[27]](/library/_a15M20)




* General principles

* The <u>IUD</u> is the most effective method of <u>emergency contraception</u> (≥ 99% <u>efficacy</u>). [[2]](/library/oB10bj0)[[24]](/library/Fa1gm20)[[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* <u>Efficacy</u> is unaffected by <u>obesity</u> and/or body weight.  [[63]](/library/_CW5un0)

* Can provide long-lasting (up to 12 years) contraception

* Timing: within 5 days of unprotected intercourse

* Mechanism of action: prevents <u>fertilization</u> and may affect the <u>oocyte</u> and <u>endometrial</u> lining  [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* Types of <u>IUDs</u>: <u>copper IUD</u> and <u>progestin IUD</u> (<u>levonorgestrel</u> 52 mg)  [[24]](/library/Fa1gm20)[[63]](/library/_CW5un0)

* Contraindications: See “<u>Contraindications to copper IUD</u>” and “<u>Contraindications to hormonal IUD</u>.” [[71]](/library/iIWJc50)

* Adverse effects: See “<u>Adverse effects and complications of IUDs</u>.”





![Intrauterine device in situ](media/u5scadhbvskjyhjj46quoigh.jpg)

Intrauterine device in situ




#### Emergency contraceptive pills (<u>ECPs</u>) [[27]](/library/_a15M20)[[68]](/library/2Y1To20)[[69]](/library/WY1PL20)




* General principles

* Do not disrupt embryo implantation or established <u>pregnancies</u>

* Significantly less effective in individuals with a <u>BMI</u> ≥ 25 or above a specified weight cut-off  [[27]](/library/_a15M20)[[63]](/library/_CW5un0)[[69]](/library/WY1PL20)

* Timing after unprotected intercourse [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* <u>Levonorgestrel</u>: most effective when taken within 3 days

* <u>Ulipristal acetate</u> and the <u>Yuzpe regimen</u> can be used within 5 days [[27]](/library/_a15M20)

* Types of <u>ECPs</u>

* Ulipristal acetate (prescription only) DOSAGE

* An <u>antiprogestin</u> that inhibits the <u>progesterone</u> <u>receptor</u> → inhibition or delay of <u>ovulation</u> and decreased <u>endometrial</u> <u>proliferation</u> → impaired <u>fertilization</u> [[1]](/library/AB1RWj0)[[27]](/library/_a15M20)[[72]](/library/dY1oL20)

* <u>Efficacy</u>: approx. 99% if taken within 5 days of unprotected intercourse [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* Repeat dosing in one cycle can be considered using <u>shared decision-making</u>.  [[63]](/library/_CW5un0)

* Levonorgestrel (emergency contraceptive) DOSAGE

* A high dose of <u>progestin</u> delays <u>ovulation</u> and impairs luteal function [[27]](/library/_a15M20)[[69]](/library/WY1PL20)[[73]](/library/zCWrun0)

* <u>Efficacy</u>: approx. 98% if given within 3 days of unprotected intercourse [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* Available over the counter, without a prescription

* Can be used multiple times in one <u>menstrual cycle</u> [[63]](/library/_CW5un0)

* Use with caution in individuals with a <u>BMI</u> ≥ 25 OR weighing â¥ 70 kg  [[63]](/library/_CW5un0)

* Yuzpe regimen (prescription only) DOSAGE [[27]](/library/_a15M20)[[70]](/library/cpWaom0)

* A combination of <u>ethinyl estradiol</u> and <u>levonorgestrel</u> → inhibits <u>LH</u> and <u>FSH</u> → prevents the <u>estrogen</u> surge → inhibits <u>LH</u> surge → prevents <u>ovulation</u>

* <u>Efficacy</u>: approx. 86% if taken within 5 days

* Contraindications

* Established <u>pregnancy</u> is the only contraindication.

* <u>Contraindications for hormonal contraceptives</u> do not apply to emergency contraceptives  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* Adverse effects of <u>ECPs</u>

* <u>Headache</u>, fatigue, <u>dizziness</u>

* <u>Nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u> [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* <u>Breast</u> tenderness

* <u>Dysmenorrhea</u>, menstrual changes





> [!TIP]
> <u>Ulipristal acetate</u> is the most effective <u>emergency contraceptive pill</u>. [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)[[69]](/library/WY1PL20)




> [!TIP]
> All individuals, including those with <u>USMEC contraindications for contraceptive methods</u>, can use <u>ECPs</u> safely and effectively. [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)




### Ongoing management after emergency contraception [[69]](/library/WY1PL20)




#### All patients




* Educate the patient on expected adverse effects.

* <u>Screen for intimate partner violence</u> and sex trafficking.  [[63]](/library/_CW5un0)[[74]](/library/axWQEn0)

* Recommend a <u>pregnancy test</u> if the next <u>menstrual period</u> is ≥ 1 week after its expected date.

* Offer <u>STI screening</u>.

* For victims of <u>sexual assault</u>: Provide <u>management of recent sexual assault</u>. [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)





#### Patients with <u>IUDs</u>




* Advise patients to return immediately if the <u>IUD</u> is expelled.

* If patients do not wish to keep the <u>IUD</u> long-term, offer to start immediate <u>hormonal contraception</u>.





#### Patients who took <u>ECPs</u>




* Offer to initiate or place a referral for a reliable method of contraception.

* If the patient desires <u>hormonal contraception</u>, educate the patient on when they may initiate or resume it.

* <u>Ulipristal</u>

* Wait 5 days after taking <u>ulipristal</u>

* Use a barrier method of contraception until the next <u>menstrual period</u>.  [[68]](/library/2Y1To20)

* <u>Levonorgestrel</u> or <u>Yuzpe regimen</u>

* Initiate immediately.

* Use a barrier method of contraception for 7 days.

## Special patient groups

### <u>Contraception in epilepsy</u>



* See “<u>Epilepsy and contraception</u>.”




### Contraception in adolescent individuals [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)[[75]](/library/rBdfXs0)[[76]](/library/jIW_c50)




* Contraception is an important component of <u>adolescent health care</u>.

* Approx. 30% of high school students are sexually active. [[75]](/library/rBdfXs0)

* Most <u>pregnancies during adolescence</u> are unintended. [[77]](/library/5JdiuI0)

* Allow minors to consent to contraception without parental notification if permitted by state laws.

* Educate <u>adolescents</u> on all forms of contraception and use <u>shared decision-making</u> when <u>initiating contraceptives</u>.  [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)

* Avoid <u>barriers to contraceptive use</u>; offer same-day procedures (e.g., implant insertion, <u>IUD</u> placement) if possible.  [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)

* Regardless of contraceptive method chosen, emphasize the role of <u>condom</u> use for <u>prevention of STIs</u>. [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)

* When short-acting methods of <u>hormonal contraception</u> are used, encourage the use of automated reminders to improve adherence.

* Regularly scheduled visits to discuss contraception and <u>reproductive and sexual health in adolescents</u> may increase adherence.

* Consider providing <u>adolescents</u> with advance prescription and counseling for <u>emergency contraceptive pills</u>.  [[70]](/library/cpWaom0)





> [!TIP]
> Use the <u>initiation of contraception</u> as a prompt to discuss healthy relationships, <u>intimate partner violence</u>, and <u>STI prevention</u> (including <u>HPV vaccination</u>). [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)




> [!WARNING]
> Be aware of all local and state laws regarding contraception for <u>adolescents</u>.




> [!TIP]
> <u>Adolescents</u> can purchase <u>progestin-only pills</u> and <u>emergency contraceptive pills</u> over the counter without parents being informed. [[14]](/library/JxdsxH0)




### Contraception in postpartum individuals [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




* <u>Progestin-only contraception</u> and <u>IUDs</u> can generally be used throughout the <u>postpartum period</u>.

* <u>Combined hormonal contraceptives</u> (<u>CHCs</u>) may be contraindicated during the <u>postpartum period</u> depending on:

* Number of days postpartum

* Presence of <u>postpartum risk factors for VTE</u>

* Whether the patient is <u>breastfeeding</u>

* Before prescribing contraception, consider any other <u>contraindications for contraceptive methods</u>.





| <br>Postpartum contraceptive options [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)<br> |  |
| --- | --- |
|  | Recommendation |
| < 21 days postpartum | <br><br>* <u>CHCs</u> are contraindicated.<br><br>* <u>IUDs</u> can be placed immediately postpartum, but there is an increased risk of expulsion.<br><br>* <u>Progestin</u>-only contraceptives are generally safe.<br><br><br> |
| 21–29 days postpartum | <br><br>* <u>Progestin</u>-only contraceptives are generally safe.<br><br>* <u>IUDs</u> may be placed.<br><br>* If <u>breastfeeding</u>: <u>CHCs</u> are not recommended.<br><br>* If not <u>breastfeeding</u>, screen for <u>postpartum risk factors for VTE</u>.<br><br>* Any <u>risk factor</u>: <u>CHCs</u> are not recommended.<br><br>* No <u>risk factors</u>: <u>CHCs</u> are generally safe.<br><br><br> |
| 30–42 days postpartum | <br><br>* <u>IUDs</u> and <u>progestin</u>-only contraceptives are safe.<br><br>* Patients with any postpartum <u>risk factor for VTE</u>: <u>CHCs</u> are not recommended.<br><br>* No <u>postpartum risk factors for VTE</u>: <u>CHCs</u> are generally safe.<br><br><br> |
| > 42 days postpartum | <br>* Follow the same recommendations for nonpostpartum individuals.<br><br> |





> [!WARNING]
> If < 21 days postpartum, avoid <u>estrogen</u>-containing <u>OCPs</u> (i.e., <u>CHCs</u>) due to the increased risk of <u>venous thromboembolism</u>. [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




> [!TIP]
> <u>CHCs</u> can decrease <u>breast milk</u> supply in some individuals; women having difficulties with <u>breastfeeding</u> may wish to consider alternative contraceptive options. [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)




### Contraception after spontaneous or induced abortion [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)[[78]](/library/UxWbDn0)




* All methods of contraception are safe to use immediately in the absence of other <u>contraindications for contraceptive methods</u>. [[8]](/library/tB1Xcj0)

* <u>IUD</u> expulsion rates may be elevated. [[78]](/library/UxWbDn0)

* If contraception is initiated > 7 days after <u>miscarriage</u> or abortion, <u>backup contraception</u> is recommended (unless a <u>copper IUD</u> has been placed).  [[6]](/library/DIW1U50)





### Contraception and <u>menopause</u>




See “<u>Contraception during perimenopause</u>.”




### Contraception in <u>transgender</u> and <u>nonbinary</u> individuals [[2]](/library/oB10bj0)[[79]](/library/mqWV_m0)




See “<u>Reproductive health care for transgender individuals</u>.”




### Contraception for underserved individuals




Patients can consider contraceptive methods available without prescription:




* <u>Condoms</u>

* <u>Spermicide</u>

* <u>Contraceptive sponge</u>

* <u>Levonorgestrel emergency contraceptive</u> pill

* Behavioral contraceptive methods

* Norgestrel <u>progesterone-only pill</u>
